title: What Does “Done” Mean?
focus: 区分开发完成和可交付，明确验收范围
story:
The green mark beside my task looks reassuring. It is the third week of my new job, and I have finally finished something that other people can see.

When a staff member changes a class time, a small window asks them to confirm. The new time then appears on the calendar. I have checked it with several test classes.

Daniel stops beside my desk. “Is the change-time work done?”

“Yes,” I say.

“Great. Can I show it this afternoon?”

My hands stay on the keyboard. “The calendar part?”

“The whole journey. Change the time, notify the learners.”

Behind him, Rui slowly removes his headphones.

“The notification work is a separate task,” I say. “I thought you meant mine.”

Daniel looks at the green mark. “It says 'change class time'.”

“It does.”

He takes a breath, then looks at his watch. “Meeting room. Ten minutes. Let's find out what we actually have.”

The room has a whiteboard with half a drawing left from another meeting. Rui wipes away a square but leaves a cloud in the corner. I bring my laptop and the uncomfortable feeling that I have passed an exam using the wrong question paper.

Daniel draws three boxes: change, save, notify.

“Where are we?”

“The change window works,” I say. “The new time is saved. I tested both. But the notification service isn't connected to this screen.”

“And if saving fails?”

“The window stays open and shows an error.”

“What does the error say?”

I show him. The message says that the action could not be completed.

“Does it tell staff whether the old time is still there?” Rui asks.

“No. It should.”

Daniel taps the third box. “Can we connect this by lunch?”

Rui looks at me, but does not answer for me.

“I can connect it,” I say slowly. “I can't say it's ready for a demonstration until we check the result.”

“What result?”

“Whether the email shows the correct old and new times. And whether only people enrolled in that class receive it.”

Daniel puts down the pen. “All right. That's more useful than just saying no.”

I want to explain that I am not saying no at all. Instead, I turn my laptop so we can all see the task description.

“Could we agree what 'done' means here?”

There is a brief silence. I hear a trolley rolling along the corridor.

Daniel pulls the keyboard towards him. “Yes. Let's write it now.”

We make a short checklist. A valid new time must be saved. If saving fails, the old time must remain and the screen must explain that. A notification must show both times clearly. The test must use enrolled test learners, not every name in the database.

Rui adds another line: another engineer must review the change.

“Me?” I ask.

“Not your own change,” he says. “I'll review yours. You'll review mine when you've learnt more of the system.”

Daniel deletes the green mark and replaces it with 'in progress'. My face warms, though nobody comments.

“Today's demonstration?” I ask.

“I'll show the calendar and explain that notifications are still being tested,” he says. “I should have checked before promising the whole journey.”

That helps, but it does not remove my part. I chose the word done because it was short and sounded confident. I could have described exactly what worked.

After the meeting, Rui returns to his desk. I follow him.

“Was my answer very bad?”

“It was incomplete.” He pulls out his chair. “Those aren't always the same thing.”

He shows me a task he completed the previous month. Under its checklist are three comments and a photograph of a handwritten calculation.

“I missed a case,” he says. “A reviewer found it.”

I read the comments. They are direct, but none says that Rui is a bad engineer.

Later, I change the error message and run the saving tests again. Then I write an update: 'Calendar change and save are working in the test environment. Email connection and review are still outstanding.'

It takes longer than typing done. Daniel replies with a thumbs-up and moves his demonstration to the smaller scope.

Before I leave, I take one final look at the task. The mark is still grey. For once, the colour is telling the truth.

Just as I reach for my coat, Daniel calls me back. He has finished the smaller demonstration. Someone from a centre has stayed on the line with a question about the calendar. Would I take it?

On his screen a woman is sitting in a room with a coat over the back of the next chair. She has written the two class times on a scrap of paper.

“Suppose I save the new time and the phone rings,” she says. “I turn to answer it. When I get back, how do I know whether anybody's been told?”

I have been thinking about the person who stays in front of the screen until the job is finished. It hasn't occurred to me that this person also answers the phone.

“In the version you saw today, nobody gets an email,” I say. “You would still have to contact people yourself.”

“Yes, I gathered that. I'm asking about the version we're waiting for.”

Daniel starts to speak, then looks at me. I could describe the email connection we mean to build. That still wouldn't answer her question.

“I don't know what you'll see when you come back to the desk,” I say. “Could we bring that question to the staff demonstration?”

“Please do. You'll have people there who spend a lot of time being interrupted.”

As if on cue, someone off screen asks her where the spare pens are. “Second drawer,” she says, without turning her head.

On the way out, Daniel holds the door for me. “I almost told her the email would have both times in it.”

“So did I.”

He takes out his phone and adds her words to the invitation draft. For once the thing we need to show somebody is the moment after the part we planned to show.

phrases.zh: 准确限定已完成的部分

phrases.en: I can connect it, but I need time to check it.
phrases.zh: 区分实现与验证所需时间

practice.grammar: 用 but 连接能力与限制：I can connect it, but I need time to check it. 先说能做到什么，再说尚缺的条件；避免只说 yes 或 no。
practice.pronunciation: 练习对比重音：The CALENDAR works, but the EMAIL connection is still outstanding. 第一遍慢读，第二遍只加强两个对比词，第三遍替换成你的工作事项。

questions.q: Why do Andy and Daniel understand “done” differently?
questions.a: Andy means the calendar task, while Daniel means the whole journey including notifications.

questions.q: Why does the centre worker ask what she will see when she returns to the desk?
questions.a: She may have to answer a phone call before checking whether learners were told.

questions.q: What will Daniel show that afternoon?
questions.a: He will show the calendar and explain that notifications are still being tested.

roleplay.context: 你是 Andy，主管以为全部功能完成了。你需要重新说明范围并提出验收标准。

turns.line: So everything is ready to show?
turns.cue: 说明日历已可用，邮件部分仍未连接。

turns.line: What exactly do you need to check?
turns.cue: 给出邮件中的时间和收件人两个检查点。

turns.line: Can I mark the whole task as done?
turns.cue: 建议保留进行中状态，并安排另一位工程师审查。

practice.transfer: 朋友请你安排一次旅行，并问“都准备好了吗？”用英语分别说明已订项目、待确认项目，以及怎样才算安排完成。
practice.retell: 先用一句话解释误会，再按“已有结果—缺少检查—共同决定”复述会议。至少使用一个 but 和一个 until。
